>>> The **sunk cost fallacy** occurs when people continue investing time, money, or effort into a decision based on what they’ve already sacrificed (the "sunk cost"), rather than evaluating the future costs and benefits objectively. Rational decisions should ignore sunk costs and focus on marginal costs and future value.

>>> **Example 1 (Business/Investment):** A company spends $5 million on a software project that is now clearly flawed and unlikely to succeed. Instead of canceling it, executives push forward to avoid "wasting" the initial investment, even though continuing will cost more money and delay better alternatives. They confuse the sunk cost (the $5M already spent) with the future cost (additional time/money) and wrongly believe the project is still viable solely because they’ve already committed heavily.

>>> **Example 2 (Personal/Relationship):** Someone stays in a toxic relationship for years because they’ve invested so much time, emotional energy, and shared history. They justify staying by thinking, *“I’ve already put so much into this; I can’t just walk away.”* The sunk cost (time and effort already spent) cloud their judgment about whether the relationship is still worth continuing, ignoring current harm and future potential.

>>> **Example 3 (Public Policy/Infrastructure):** A government funds a costly highway project that is environmentally damaging and economically inefficient. Despite clear evidence that the project will not achieve its stated goals, officials continue funding it because “we’ve already spent billions,” even though the rational choice might be to redirect funds to better projects. The sunk cost (past spending) becomes a reason to persist, even when future costs outweigh future benefits.
